claim: Luo et al. use iterative LQG to learn time-varying operational-space wrench policies inside a low-gain motion/force controller, yielding an implicit variable-impedance behavior for four tight-tolerance gear-assembly subtasks on a Sawyer robot. In five post-training trials per task, the force-based controller achieves 5/5, 5/5, 2/5, and 4/5 successes while kinematic and direct-torque iLQG baselines are nearly always unsuccessful. A force-aware guided-policy-search neural controller generalizes modestly to 1-5 cm fixture shifts, but it does not consistently outperform its local iLQG teacher and a naive early force-input architecture fails 0/10. The work provides no convergence, stability, passivity, collision-safety, or force-limit theorem; policies are task-specific, samples are very small, some successful behaviors use large contact forces, and the claimed Pfaffian-constraint learning is an interpretation rather than an identified constraint model.
claim_locator: Section V-A/B, Table I and Figures 4-6
epistemic_status: qualified: the hardware training protocol and small-sample success counts are directly reported; adaptive impedance and constraint-learning claims describe observed/local policy behavior, not a formally identified impedance law or certified stable/passive controller
problem_and_setting: A robot must complete four contact-rich gear-assembly steps with tolerances below 0.1 mm despite movable parts, friction, and pose uncertainty. Sparse pose costs and direct torque actions make local RL prone to failure, motivating an operational-space force action representation and a global force-aware policy.
method_or_mechanism: A low-gain joint-space position loop is combined with an operational wrench term and nullspace torque. Local iLQG repeatedly fits linear-Gaussian dynamics around rollouts and optimizes a maximum-entropy linear-Gaussian wrench policy. Because the learned wrench varies with robot state, the authors interpret free-space motion as high impedance and contact probing as higher admittance, and describe the policy as implicitly learning task constraints. Mirror-descent guided policy search distills one local controller into a neural network; filtered wrist force/torque is injected only near the output layer to avoid spurious free-space coupling. Each assembly subtask is trained independently.
content_summary: The paper evaluates a force-action representation for high-precision assembly. Sawyer is commanded at 20 Hz, with four rollouts per iteration; success typically appears after three iterations and learning is said to converge after five. The cost penalizes mismatch between a three-point end-effector plane and its target. In five evaluation trials, kinematics fails all tasks, direct-torque iLQG succeeds once only on the easiest task, and the proposed controller succeeds in all trials for the first two tasks and partially for the harder square-shaft and gear-teeth tasks. Learned sequences include contact probing, maintaining downward force, rotation, and force relaxation. Generalization tests shift the base by 1, 2, or 5 cm: the proposed neural policy scores 9/10, 8/10, and 6/10 versus local iLQG 8/10, 5/10, and 6/10. Feeding force at the first network layer scores 0/10 and causes random free-space motion. No confidence intervals or formal stability analysis are supplied.
synthesis_role: Represents task-specific model-based RL using operational force actions to make precision assembly learnable. It supplies concrete hardware success/failure counts and architectural ablations, while showing that empirical compliance is not equivalent to a certified variable-impedance controller.
development_link: Compared with direct joint-torque iLQG, an operational wrench action embeds useful task structure and sharply improves small-sample hardware success. Compared with classical force/impedance control, RL selects a stochastic time-varying wrench rather than analytically scheduling stiffness/damping. Compared with passivity-constrained learning, no safety projection or energy condition restricts exploration or deployment.

evidence.finding: The implemented action is an operational-space wrench inside a low-gain joint position loop; variable impedance is implicit in the learned state-dependent wrench policy rather than an explicitly optimized stiffness/damping matrix.
Local iLQG iteratively fits linearized dynamics from rollouts and computes maximum-entropy linear-Gaussian feedback wrench policies using local quadratic cost approximations.
The authors interpret learned operational forces as implicitly improving Pfaffian task constraints, but no constraint matrix is estimated or validated directly.
Mirror-descent guided policy search trains a neural policy from the local controller, injecting low-pass-filtered force/torque near the output rather than into the first layer.
Across five trials per task, the proposed controller scores 5/5, 5/5, 2/5, and 4/5; kinematic baselines score 0/5 throughout and direct-torque iLQG baselines score at most 1/5.

One successful insertion shows exploration variance changing by phase and measured force/torque peaks at contact; aggressive downward force and contact probing are described as automatically discovered behavior.

For 1/2/5 cm shifts, the late-force neural policy scores 9/10, 8/10, and 6/10, local iLQG scores 8/10, 5/10, and 6/10, and the first-layer force architecture fails 0/10 with undesirable free-space behavior.

boundary_conditions: Each of the four assembly stages has a separately trained policy; multiplying per-stage rates is not evidence of an independently measured end-to-end assembly rate.
Training uses four rollouts per iteration and evaluation uses only five trials per assembly task and ten per generalization shift, yielding high binomial uncertainty.
The controller assumes slow robot motion and neglects acceleration and velocity terms in its operational force derivation.
Variable impedance is implicit and piecewise local; explicit positive-definite stiffness/damping trajectories are neither identified nor constrained.
The global neural policy is distilled from a single local controller, so tests examine nearby base shifts rather than broad task or object transfer.
The learned neural controller does not consistently beat local iLQG and equals it at the largest reported shift.
No analytical learning convergence, closed-loop stability, passivity, force/torque bound, collision constraint, or safe-exploration guarantee is provided.
Results concern one Sawyer, one benchmark gear set, 20 Hz control, and a manually shaped plane-distance cost.
assumptions: Operational wrench actions and the low-gain position loop restrict learning to a locally useful and physically executable behavior space.
Local linear-Gaussian dynamics approximations remain adequate over each iLQG rollout update.
Sparse target-plane distance is a sufficient cost to induce safe and successful assembly without explicit contact or force penalties.
Wrist force/torque signals after low-pass filtering contain transferable contact-phase information despite being non-Markovian.
The guided-policy-search supervised objective preserves the useful behavior of the local controller under nearby fixture shifts.
Large downward force and exploratory stochasticity remain within safe hardware and part limits in the reported experiments.
Independent per-task training and fixed initial grasp/scene conditions adequately represent the intended assembly workflow.

reported: Kinematic control fails all five trials on every task and direct-torque iLQG almost always fails without extensive cost shaping.
The proposed controller succeeds in only 2/5 trials on square-hole insertion and 4/5 on gear-teeth alignment.
Adding force/torque to the direct-torque iLQG state gives no reliable improvement because the signals are non-Markovian.
Putting force/torque at the first neural-network layer fails all generalization trials and can generate random undesirable free-space motion.
The neural policy does not consistently outperform its local iLQG controller and has high outcome variance.
inferred: A sparse pose cost can reward completion while overlooking excessive force, impact, part wear, or near-failure contact trajectories.
Local dynamics fitting and 20 Hz updates may fail under faster impacts, different friction, or more compliant parts.
Stochastic exploratory actions on hardware are not protected by a passivity or safety filter.
Calling the behavior variable impedance or learned Pfaffian constraints can overstate what is actually a state-dependent wrench policy.
Small success counts and task-specific training leave uncertainty about repeatability, end-to-end yield, and transfer to other assemblies.
